Base Threat: Uencrypted data can be intercepted in transit
Model Threat: The WebSocket communication between M1, M2, and M3 on the 'public access LAN' may not be encrypted (i.e., using `ws://` instead of `wss://`). An attacker on the LAN can passively sniff this traffic and capture the raw video frames and OCR results. Complete loss of confidentiality for all data processed by the system, including potentially sensitive visual information and text.

Base Threat: Dos attack on all IoTEdge Modules since there is no Authentication
Model Threat: An attacker who has stolen an Azure connection string (e.g., for Cognitive Services) can run a script to make an unlimited number of API calls. This will rapidly consume the service's monthly quota or incur a very large bill. Legitimate requests from the IoT device will be throttled or blocked, and the service owner will face a significant financial impact.

Base Threat: Application Insights is connected via Connection String which is stored in .env file on the IoTEdge device. Once user gains access to the device, .env file can be read and attacker can tamper the log data.
Model Threat: Since modules communicate via WebSockets on a public access LAN, an attacker can perform a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack to intercept and alter the data flowing between M1, M2, and M3. For example, they could modify the video frames in transit. The system processes altered data, leading to incorrect OCR and Text-to-Speech results. Confidential information in the video could be replaced or manipulated.

Base Threat: Application Insights is connected via Connection String which is stored in .env file on the IoTEdge device. Once user gains access to the device, .env file can be read and attacker can tamper the log data.
Model Threat: An attacker with access to the IoT Edge device's local storage could modify the container images for M1, M2, or M3 that were deployed by the CI/CD pipeline. The next time the module starts, it will run the attacker's tampered code. Complete compromise of the module's functionality, data exfiltration, or using the module as a pivot point to attack other systems.

Model Threat: An attacker on the 'public access LAN' can send crafted WebSocket messages to M2 or M3, pretending to be a legitimate upstream module (e.g., spoofing M1 to M2). This could be used to inject malicious or fabricated data into the processing pipeline. Generation of incorrect audio output, pollution of debug data in Azure Storage, or triggering unintended actions in downstream modules.
